title: Seals Are Secret Ocean Scientists!
summary: What if you could put a tiny backpack on a seal and it would explore the ocean for you? That's exactly what scientists are doing in Antarctica! Oceanographer Lily Dove studies the Southern Ocean, the huge ocean around Antarctica. But instead of diving herself, she used data from seals. These seals wear small sensors on their foreheads. The sensors measure temperature, saltiness, and pressure. The seals dive more than 100 meters (330 feet) deep — way deeper than most human divers can go safely. "They're oceanographers," Dove says. "They are regularly making dives in areas that we don't often get to sample." The seals don't mind wearing the sensors. They just go about their day, hunting for food. While they swim, they collect important clues about how climate change is heating up the ocean. Now Dove works with robots called gliders. She can control them from Georgia, thousands of miles away! But she says seals are more independent. "Seals very much tell me where they want to go," she laughs. Thanks to these furry helpers, we're learning how the ocean stores heat — heat that can stay trapped for hundreds of years.
why_it_matters: The ocean's heat affects the weather you feel, the beaches you visit and even how high the seas rise — so learning about it now helps people plan for the future.

background_read: Antarctica is the coldest continent on Earth and holds most of the world's fresh water frozen as ice. The Southern Ocean around it is one of the least-studied parts of the planet because it is so cold and far away.

Scientists have found that the ocean soaks up most of the extra heat trapped by climate change, which is why measuring ocean temperatures matters so much. That heat does not vanish — it can stay in the water for centuries and affects weather everywhere.
Oceanographers often use robots called gliders to explore under the ice, because ships cannot always go where seals can.
Article_Structure: WHO: Oceanographer Lily Dove and the seals of Antarctica that carry sensors
WHAT: The seals collect data on temperature, saltiness and pressure as they dive, helping scientists study how the ocean stores heat
WHERE: The Southern Ocean around Antarctica, with Dove controlling gliders remotely from Georgia
WHY: The ocean's trapped heat is linked to climate change and can stay in the water for hundreds of years, so understanding it matters for everyone

perspectives.description: They are delighted because seals reach deep, icy places that ships and people rarely visit, giving free data that would be very expensive to collect otherwise.
They want to be sure the sensors are light and harmless, since the seals are wild animals just trying to hunt for food.
They see this as useful evidence about how fast the ocean is warming, which can push leaders to act sooner.
